intro: Stand at the corner of State and Madison in Chicago and everything you see is human geography. The people passing speak Spanish, Polish, English, Arabic and Mandarin. The buildings sit on ground that was a swamp two centuries ago. The trains underfoot follow lines laid down for cattle and grain. The lake at the end of the street is why the city is here at all. Human geography asks the questions behind that scene: why people live where they live, why they speak and believe what they do, why they move, how they feed and power their cities, and where the lines fall that divide one place from another.

This unit works with real numbers and real maps. You will read population pyramids for Japan and Nigeria and see two very different futures in the bars. You will follow the Great Migration into Chicago's South Side, trace language families from Iceland to Bangladesh, and put the world's religions on a map. You will climb to the top of the Willis Tower and read the city below as rings, wedges and rail lines. You will ask where the world's food, water and energy come from, who goes without, and what the climate record shows.

By the end you should be able to explain why one country grows while another shrinks, why migrants go where they go, how a city sorts itself, why Illinois grows corn and Florida grows oranges, what development means and how it is measured, and how borders both cause conflict and make cooperation possible. Chicago will be the case study at every step, because almost every pattern in the world shows up somewhere in this one city.
bigQuestion: What shapes where people live, how they live, and how they divide the Earth among themselves?

timeline.t: The Land Ordinance lays a square-mile grid across the Midwest that Illinois fields still follow
Thomas Malthus warns that population will outrun food
Illinois becomes a state, with its northern border moved up to reach Lake Michigan
The Chicago Board of Trade opens and begins setting the price of the world's grain
Ernst Ravenstein publishes his laws of migration from British census data
Engineers reverse the Chicago River to keep sewage out of Lake Michigan
The Great Migration brings about six million Black Americans north, many to Chicago
Ernest Burgess draws Chicago as concentric rings, the first modern model of a city
Norman Borlaug wins the Nobel Peace Prize for the Green Revolution
The United Nations publishes the first Human Development Index
For the first time, more than half of humanity lives in cities

words.d: the number of people living in a given area of land
the shift from high birth and death rates to low ones as a society industrializes
the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime
a condition such as war or drought that drives people to leave a place
a condition such as jobs or safety that attracts people to a place
a group of languages descended from a common ancestor
a religion that seeks converts from anyone anywhere
the visible marks a culture leaves on the land
the growth in the share of people living in cities
farming run as a large industry linked to seed, machinery, trading and food companies
a United Nations measure combining income, life expectancy and years of schooling
a state whose population is mostly one nation with a shared identity

test.q: Which country's population pyramid has a very wide base and a narrow top?
test.why: Nigeria's median age is about eighteen and women have roughly five children each, so the bottom bars are enormous.

test.q: Why did the world's population grow so fast during the twentieth century?
choices: Death rates fell while birth rates stayed high for a time
test.why: Stage two of the demographic transition, falling deaths with unchanged births, produced the growth.

test.q: A total fertility rate of about 2.1 is called replacement level because
choices: It keeps a population roughly the same size over time
Every couple must have exactly two children by law
It is the lowest rate possible
test.why: Two children replace two parents, with a small extra for those who die young.

test.q: In Lee's model of migration, a border wall or the cost of a plane ticket is
test.why: Obstacles lie between origin and destination and make the move harder.

test.q: Which was a PUSH factor in the Great Migration?
choices: The boll weevil destroying cotton crops
Relatives already on the South Side
test.why: The boll weevil wiped out the thin living sharecroppers had, driving them out of the South.

test.q: English reached North America mainly through
test.why: English speakers physically moved across the Atlantic and settled.

test.q: Which pair of religions is universalizing?
test.why: Christianity and Islam seek converts everywhere; the others are mostly tied to one people and place.

test.q: Which best explains why some ethnically diverse countries are peaceful and others are not?
choices: Whether power is shared and groups are treated fairly
Whether the country is an island
test.why: Switzerland and Chicago show diversity alone does not cause conflict; fair treatment and political choices decide.

test.q: Girls' schooling matters for development because women who finish secondary school tend to
choices: Have fewer children and see more of them survive
test.why: Education is the strongest predictor of lower fertility and better child survival.

test.q: Chicago grew rapidly in the 1800s mainly because of its
choices: Site, the solid dry ground it was built on
Situation, at the link between the Great Lakes and Mississippi systems
test.why: The site was a muddy swamp; the situation, where water routes and later railroads met, made the city.

test.q: Burgess's 1925 model described a city as
choices: Concentric rings around a central business district
test.why: Burgess drew Chicago as a bull's-eye of rings, with newcomers in the zone nearest the Loop.

test.q: Most of the corn grown in Illinois
choices: Is eaten as corn on the cob
Becomes ethanol fuel or animal feed
test.why: Illinois corn mostly goes to ethanol, livestock feed and export, not directly to dinner plates.

test.q: Since the 1970s, many Rust Belt factories closed because
choices: Cheaper shipping and communications let companies move production to lower-cost countries
test.why: The global division of labor sent each stage of production wherever it was cheapest.

test.q: Why is famine today almost always found in places with war?
choices: Because the world does not grow enough food
Because wars only happen in deserts
Because soldiers eat all the food
Because fighting stops planting, cuts roads and blocks aid
test.why: Enough food exists globally; war and poverty keep it from reaching people.

test.q: In geography, a nation without a state is best illustrated by
test.why: The Kurds share a common identity but are split among Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria with no state of their own.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Is Chicago's history mainly a story of good situation (location) or of human choices? Support it with at least three pieces of evidence from this unit, such as the portage, the river reversal, the Great Migration, the stockyards, the steel mills, or the ward and covenant lines.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start.
Use specific evidence with dates and numbers from the unit: Chicago's growth from 4,500 to 1.7 million, the 1900 reversal, the Black population figures, the closing of South Works.
Explain your reasoning: show how each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just that it exists.
Address the other side: name the strongest evidence for the opposite view and explain why your claim still holds.
End by saying what your answer suggests about cities in general.
